newsitem.title: USA: ValuJet exec blames contractor for error.
newsitem.headline: ValuJet exec blames contractor for error.

text.p: A ValuJet executive on Wednesday shifted responsibility to a maintenance contractor for a crucial mistake that allowed hazardous oxygen canisters to be shipped aboard doomed ValuJet Flight 592 without safety caps.

Under rigorous questioning from federal aviation experts, David Gentry, ValuJet vice president of heavy maintenance, said he believed SabreTech Corp. was responsible for installing the safety caps, the first of a series of errors that may have resulted in a raging fire aboard the jet.

The testimony came on the third day of a National Transportation Safety Board public hearing into the crash of the ValuJet DC-9, which went down on May 11 in Florida's Everglades, killing all 110 passengers and crew on board.
During a break in the hearing, relatives of the ValuJet victims held a news conference to criticize federal aviation inspectors and call for tougher safety standards.

Crash investigators zeroed in on the critical failure of SabreTech mechanics to install safety caps on the oxygen generators when they were taken off several ValuJet MD-80 aircraft. The generators were eventually loaded into the forward cargo hold of Flight 592.
Investigators believe the canisters may have started or fueled a fire that roared through the jet about five minutes after takeoff from Miami International Airport.

Investigators have indicated through their questioning at the hearing that they consider the failure to put safety caps on the oxygen generators perhaps the crucial error that might have led to an inferno on board the jet.

Gentry, who testified for more than two hours, said ValuJet was responsible for the airworthiness of its aircraft no matter who had done the work on them. But he said when an airplane went into a licensed repair shop, the responsibility to ensure that the work was done properly rested with the contractor.
Later, under insistent questioning, Gentry conceded that ValuJet had ultimate responsibility for the work done by outside contractors on its planes.

On Monday SabreTech president Steven Townes said that the mechanics who removed the canisters had not completed the work and the works cards which instructed the mechanics to install safety caps had been improperly signed off.

Gentry also said that with several hundred mechanics working on an airplane, it was impossible for ValuJet's technical representatives who oversaw work at SabreTech to check that every task had been completed properly.

But investigators questioned whether ValuJet employed enough technical representatives to oversee SabreTech's work. Gentry said three representatives, along with two part-timers, oversaw work that was done 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

Relatives of crash victims, speaking as a group for the first time since the hearing began, said they wanted to see smoke detectors and fire suppression equipment installed in cargo holds and improved hazardous materials training for airline workers.
"This airplane disaster was not pilot error, it was not due to weather. It was due to total negligence and even possible criminal negligence," said Amanda Myers, who lost her parents in the crash.
